title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who faced U.S. deportation efforts and 'vindictive prosecution,' arrives in Spain
summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the U.S., arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the United States, potentially ending a…

image.caption: Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrives at Madrid's airport after leaving the United States, on Wednesday. (Francisco Seco/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the U.S., arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the United States, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
Trump administration celebrates 31-year-old's departure after nearly 2-year legal saga
Abrego Garcia was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to an El Salvador prison despite never having been convicted of a crime in the U.S.

Protracted legal battles ensued. A judge accused U.S. President Donald Trump's administration of "bad faith" when it said it was helpless to adhere a court order to return him from the notorious CECOT prison to the U.S.
Abrego Garcia was only returned in June 2025 when federal officials charged him with a series of offences including human smuggling in relation to a 2022 incident in Tennessee.

That case fell apart, with a federal judge this past May saying it reflected an "abuse of prosecuting power" from the government. He granted Abrego Garcia's motion to dismiss for "selective or vindictive prosecution."

Abrego Garcia and his wife Jennifer Vasquez Sura, right, leave the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in Greenbelt, Md., following a Oct. 6 hearing. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)

Abrego Garcia, married and a father of a young child, later expressed his willingness to be deported to Costa Rica, which had agreed to accept him. However, the Trump administration refused, attempting to send him to Africa, part of its third-country deportation efforts that have been condemned by international human rights organizations.
Abrego Garcia, his lawyers and the Trump administration sought to portray the departure as a victory.

"I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom," Abrego Garcia said in a statement. "I am leaving with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me, believed in me, and joined my family in this fight."
Abrego Garcia didn't speak to reporters after landing at Madrid's main international airport on Wednesday, and raised a fist as he entered a van.

blocks.text: Lawyer hopes Abrego Garcia can return to U.S.

The Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that Abrego Garcia self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn't receive any incentives and won't be allowed back in to the U.S.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was "delighted" about Abrego Garcia's departure, listing off a litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation Abrego Garcia has repeatedly denied.
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, called this a temporary departure as he "waits out the end of this administration." He said Abrego Garcia has many options to return to U.S.

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," he said.

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia at the El Salvadoran mega-prison, described him as a "free man" and said he is travelling to a country of his choice.
"I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration's constant persecution," he said in a statement.
The 31-year-old Abrego Garcia has lived in Maryland for years as an unauthorized resident after entering the country as a teenager.

In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

Abrego Garcia's deportation in early 2025 came as the Trump administration was ramping up its immigration crackdown, promising to deport one million people annually. Democrats have slammed the efforts, pointing to widespread arrests of people not accused of committing a crime in the U.S. Deaths of individuals in immigration detention have also increased compared to past administrations.

When Abrego Garcia was deported, an official from the Trump administration called the move an "administrative error," but the president and El Salvador's autocratic leader Nayib Bukele celebrated the deportation of migrants from the U.S. to the Latin American prison. Trump encouraged Bukele to build more prisons.

The administration also widely communicated that Abrego Garcia's wife Jennifer Vasquez Sura, a U.S. citizen, sought a protection order from him in both 2020 and 2021. He was never arrested, and Vasquez Sura withdrew the order, saying the couple had entered counselling.

Later in Abrego Garcia's legal saga, Todd Lyons, then acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said that deporting Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be "prejudicial to the United States."
Trump encourages El Salvador to build more prisons to house deportees from U.S.
Lyons wrote that Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the U.S. has spent governmental resources and political capital in negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals.

His case took an unusual turn on Oct. 6 when, five minutes before a hearing expected to determine whether ICE could detain and deport him to the West African country of Liberia, attorneys for both sides left the courtroom, along with Abrego Garcia.

blocks.text: When they returned 15 minutes later, it was announced the hearing was cancelled. The two sides then gathered for another 90 minutes before leaving the courthouse without explanation.

The U.S. Supreme Court is scheduled in the current session that runs through June 2027 to hear a number of cases that could alter the framework of the country's immigration and asylum system, including one that concerns third-country deportations.
